title: My Father Died In Florida In 2017 And My Stepbrother Craig Promised To Handle All The Paperwork, But Seven Years Later A Social Security Worker Told Me Dad Was Still Receiving $2,140 Every Month, More Than $180,000 Deposited Into An Account
excerpt: My father, Raymond Pierce, died in October of 2017 in Port Charlotte, Florida. He was eighty-four. He had congestive heart failure, and the end came slowly, then all at once.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — ALL THE PAPERWORK
My father, Raymond Pierce, died in October of 2017 in Port Charlotte, Florida. He was eighty-four. He had congestive heart failure, and the end came slowly, then all at once.

I live in Bend, Oregon. Dad and my mother divorced when I was fifteen, after twenty-two years of marriage. A few years later, he married a woman named Darlene, who had a son from her first marriage. That son was my stepbrother, Craig. Darlene died in 2012. After that, Craig moved into Dad’s house in Port Charlotte to “help out.”

I won’t pretend Craig and I were close. He was eight years younger than me, and we had never lived under the same roof. But in those last years, he was the one who was there. He drove Dad to cardiology appointments. He picked up prescriptions. He was the one who answered the phone at three in the morning when Dad fell. I was three thousand miles away with a job and two teenagers. I was grateful to him. Truly.

When Dad died, I flew to Florida for the funeral. It was small. A few of Dad’s old friends from the Navy. Some neighbors. Craig stood next to me at the graveside, and afterward he put his arm around my shoulders.
“Don’t worry about anything, Lisa,” he said. “I’ll handle all the paperwork. The bank, the house, Social Security, all of it. You’ve got enough on your plate.”

I remember feeling such relief. Paperwork after a death is overwhelming, especially from three thousand miles away. Dad’s estate was small anyway. His house had a reverse mortgage. His savings were mostly gone after years of medical bills. There wasn’t much to fight over, and I didn’t want to fight.
So I said thank you, and I flew home, and I trusted Craig.
For seven years, I didn’t think about it again. I grieved my father. I raised my kids. I assumed, the way anyone would, that a dead man’s Social Security checks stop when he dies.
Don’t worry about anything. I’ll handle all the paperwork. You’ve got enough on your plate.
PART 2 — THE WOMAN AT SOCIAL SECURITY

Last spring, my mother, who is now seventy-nine and lives near me in Oregon, finally decided to look into survivor benefits. I didn’t know this until recently, but if you were married to someone for at least ten years, you can sometimes collect survivor benefits on their record after they die, even if you divorced. My parents were married for twenty-two years. My mother’s own benefit was small. Her survivor benefit on Dad’s record would be larger.
I took a morning off work and drove her to the Social Security office in Bend. We waited an hour and a half. Then we sat down with a kind, efficient woman named Mrs. Okafor.
My mother handed over her marriage certificate, her divorce decree, and a copy of my father’s death certificate. Mrs. Okafor typed in Dad’s information to pull up his record. Then she stopped typing.
She frowned at her screen. She typed again. She frowned harder.
“Ma’am,” she said to me carefully, “this says your father is still receiving benefits.”
I actually laughed. “That’s impossible. He died in 2017. I was at his funeral.”
My mother held up the death certificate. Mrs. Okafor looked at it. She looked at her screen. She looked at the death certificate again.

“Our records show your father as living,” she said slowly. “And his benefits have been paid every month since 2017. Directly deposited.” She turned the screen slightly toward me. “Two thousand one hundred and forty dollars a month.”
I did the math right there in the chair. Seven years. Eighty-some months.
More than one hundred and eighty thousand dollars.
My mother put her hand on my arm. Neither of us said anything. Mrs. Okafor’s face had changed. She was no longer a clerk processing a claim. She was someone who had just found something very wrong.
“Excuse me,” she said, standing up. “I need to get my supervisor.”
Our records show your father as living. His benefits have been paid every month since 2017.
PART 3 — A SECOND NAME ON THE ACCOUNT
The supervisor’s name was Mr. Delgado. He sat down with us in a small private office and went through everything slowly.

He confirmed that Social Security had never received a report of my father’s death. Normally, he explained, the funeral home files the death certificate electronically with the state, and the state reports the death to Social Security automatically. Benefits stop within a month or two. Most families never have to do anything.
Mr. Delgado looked at my copy of the death certificate. He looked at it for a long time. Then he took a pen and circled something.
It was my father’s Social Security number. Printed on his official death certificate. One digit was wrong. A seven where there should have been a one.
“Who gave the funeral home this information?” he asked.
I looked at the box on the certificate marked “Informant.” The person who provides the deceased’s personal details to the funeral director. The name in the box was Craig Mason. Stepson.

With the wrong number, the death report went into the system and never matched my father’s record. As far as the federal government was concerned, Raymond Pierce was still alive, still eighty-something, still living in Florida, and still entitled to his monthly check.

Mr. Delgado checked. The deposits had gone into Dad’s old checking account at a bank in Port Charlotte. The same account they had always gone into. “There’s a second name on the account,” he said. “A joint account holder. Craig Mason.”
I drove my mother home in silence. When we got there, she made me a cup of tea and sat across from me at her kitchen table.
“Call him,” she said. “Before you do anything else. Give him the chance to tell you it’s a mistake.”
One digit was wrong. A seven where there should have been a one.
PART 4 — THE PHONE CALL
I called Craig that night. I hadn’t spoken to him in about three years. He answered on the fourth ring, cheerful.
“Lisa! Wow, long time. How are the kids?”
I didn’t make small talk. I told him exactly what Social Security had told me. Dad listed as alive. Seven years of deposits. The joint account. His name.
There was a long silence. Then Craig said, very smoothly, “I had no idea. That must be some kind of bank error.”
“A bank error that lasted seven years?” I said.
“I never even look at that account,” he said. “I forgot it was still open. I’ve been so busy. I’ll call the bank tomorrow and get it straightened out.”
“Craig, there’s a hundred and eighty thousand dollars.”
“Well, I’m sure it’s all still sitting there,” he said. “I’ll make sure it all goes back.”
I wanted to believe him. I really did. He had been there for Dad when I wasn’t. I had spent seven years feeling guilty about that and grateful to him. It is a hard thing to let go of gratitude.
“What about the death certificate?” I asked. “You were the informant. You gave them the Social Security number. It’s wrong.”
He laughed, a little too fast. “Lisa, I was a mess that week. My stepfather had just died. I probably typed it wrong. I’m not perfect.”
I let him go. I told myself he might be telling the truth.
Two days later, Mr. Delgado from Social Security called me back. He said he had something else to tell me, and he needed me to sit down.
“In 2020,” he said, “someone called our office pretending to be your father.”
In 2020, someone called our office pretending to be your father.
PART 5 — THE CALL IN 2020

Social Security keeps records of every contact on an account. In August of 2020, during the pandemic, when most offices were closed and almost everything was done by phone, someone had called the national Social Security number claiming to be Raymond Pierce.
The caller answered all the security questions. Date of birth. Mother’s maiden name. Place of birth. Then he asked to update his mailing address.
The new address was in Valdosta, Georgia.

The reverse mortgage on Dad’s house in Port Charlotte had come due after his death, of course. The bank took the house in 2019. Craig had to move out. And instead of reporting Dad’s death and closing everything up, he had called Social Security, pretended to be an eighty-seven-year-old dead man, and moved Dad’s address to his own new apartment in Georgia.

So the annual letters about benefit increases would go to him. So any questions from the government would come to him. So nothing would ever reach anyone who might ask why a dead man was still getting checks.
